canonicalTopic: The List of Ai Insiders Sounding the Alarm on Their Own Companies Keeps Growing

sourceSignals.query: The List of Ai Insiders Sounding the Alarm on Their Own Companies Keeps Growing
sourceSignals.contentSnippet: Last week, OpenAI safety leader David Robinson resigned from the company, becoming the latest to join what is, in his words , a “parade of former colleagues” who have left roles at AI companies amid concerns about the tech or its use. In a subsequent essay for The Atlantic , he said the "trial and error" approach favored by AI companies must end. Robinson is far from alone. Here’s a list of other AI researchers and employees who’ve made public warnings about their former employers. ED NEWTON-REX In November 2023, Ed Newton-Rex left his role leading the audio team at Stability AI , the maker of text-to-image tool Stable Diffusion, over concerns about the way copyrighted material was being used to train the tech. "My opinion here doesn’t align with the generative AI industry’s current way of doing things,” Newton-Rex told Fast Company following his resignation, adding that he thought the industry's prevailing outlook, paired with rapidly advancing tech, would be “very, very bad for creators.” Since then, he's founded Fairly Trained , a nonprofit that issues certifications for AI companies whose data use meets certain requirements. THE GROUP LETTER On June 4, 2024, 13 current and former employees of top AI companies published a letter titled "A Right to Warn about Advanced Artificial Intelligence." In it, they asserted that the technology poses risks ranging from “the further entrenchment of existing inequalities, to manipulation and misinformation, to the loss of control of autonomous AI systems potentially resulting in human extinction,” and expressed concerns about a lack of oversight. Signatories included former Google DeepMind employee Ramana Kumar, former Anthropic and current Google DeepMind employee Neel Nanda , who leads the company’s mechanistic interpretability team; and 11 current and former OpenAI employees, including Jacob Hilton, who now works for the Alignment Research Center ; Daniel Kokotajlo, who founded and leads the nonprofit research group AI Futures Project ; William Saunders, Carroll Wainwright, and Daniel Ziegler, the latter of whom now works for Anthropic; and six people who remained anonymous. Prominent computer scientists Yoshua Bengio , Stuart Russell , and "Godfather of AI" Geoffrey Hinton also endorsed the letter. JAN LEIKE In May 2024, OpenAI Superalignment team lead Jan Leike announced his departure on X, stating that “safety culture and processes have taken a backseat to shiny products.” Leike, who has also worked at Google's DeepMind, now heads Anthropic’s alignment team. "Now is a good time to build institutional mechanisms to pace the frontier of AI development," he said on X in September. "The industry is locked into an all-out scaling race to build superintelligence as quickly as possible, and we may need to give everyone more time for safety and alignment mitigations." Leike added, “I'm not the only one who believes this," linking to a statement titled "Pacing the Frontier" signed by 1,386 employees of major AI companies. SUCHIR BALAJI After graduating from the University of California, Berkeley, Suchir Balaji was hired by OpenAI, where he spent about four years working on ChatGPT and other projects. He left the company in August 2024, on the same day as cofounder John Schulman , who said the timing was coincidental. Balaji blew the whistle on what he said were copyright infringements by Open AI, and published an essay online explaining how he thought ChatGPT's outputs violated Fair Use law. That November, he was named as a potential witness in The New York Times ’s lawsuit against OpenAI alleging willful copyright infringement. The 26-year-old was found dead in his San Francisco apartment eight days later. His death was ruled a suicide, though his parents and others raised questions about that determination, as reported by The Guardian . MRINANK SHARMA  In February, Mrinank Sharma announced his departure from Anthropic, where he led the Safeguards Research team . "I continuously find myself reckoning with our situation," Sharma wrote in his resignation letter, which he shared on X. "The world is in peril," he continued, not just from AI and bioweapons, but "a whole series of interconnected crises." ALEX TURNER Alex Turner left his job as a Google DeepMind research scientist in June, after a failed campaign to stop the company from signing a contract that allows the U.S. Pentagon to use its AI “for any lawful government purpose,” which he and others worry may allow for mass surveillance and autonomous weapons.  Last month, he testified for a U.S. Senate hearing on rogue AI. "Often we think about the movements of our overseas adversaries, but now we must consider how we may be building adversaries at home by training misaligned AI systems," he said in his written statement. JACOB COXON Jacob Coxon, a former researcher for OpenAI and Anthropic, resigned from the latter last month.  "Neither company is acting responsibly," he said in a viral X post . "They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives." He went on to assert that "the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade." In an interview with PBS in September, Coxon said an AI race with China "could be very bad, and that we should be taking pretty rapid actions for international coordination," but that he believes the company leaders echoing that desire "are privately quite skeptical" of being able to achieve that cooperation. MIKITA BALESNI, TOMEK KORBAK, AND JASMINE WANG Last week, three OpenAI safety and alignment researchers were fired for mishandling sensitive misinformation, which one of them, Tomek Korbak, said online was due to how he'd communicated information to METR , the AI research nonprofit investigating OpenAI's recent Hugging Face hacking incident . "AI is not a normal technology, and OpenAI is not a normal company," the researchers said in the letter they sent to company leadership, which they published online on October 8. "Those of us who work on safety see risks before anyone else, and we rely on close collaboration with outside experts to work out how to address them. The freedom to do so without fear, and to have well-defined internal procedures that enable this work, is itself an essential safety mechanism." OpenAI released a statement the following day saying the researchers were fired after an internal investigation "found they violated clear policies on handling sensitive information,” adding, "We want to be very clear that these decisions were not about raising safety concerns or speaking out.”

canonicalTopic: Can Ai Be Moral Without Being Sentient

sourceSignals.query: Can Ai Be Moral Without Being Sentient
sourceSignals.contentSnippet: Pope Leo XIV and one of the world’s leading AI companies recently found themselves on opposite sides of a thorny question: Can a chatbot have a conscience? A New York Times investigation published late last month revealed that Anthropic cofounder Chris Olah proposed withdrawing from a Vatican event to launch Pope Leo XIV’s first encyclical after reading an advance copy, which rejected the possibility of sentient AI. Paragraph 99 of Magnifica Humanitas states bluntly that AI models “do not undergo experiences, do not possess a body, do not feel joy or pain.” Nor do they “have a moral conscience.” The disagreement reflects a widening debate over whether AI systems could, or should, ever achieve moral personhood. Anthropic spent months consulting religious scholars and ethicists about the possibility of AI consciousness, and about how to instill moral values in its models. But the Vatican—and many secular thinkers—maintain that while AI may imitate human intelligence and moral judgment (a chatbot might generate sound ethical advice without understanding its consequences), genuine morality is unique to the human experience . The debate has implications far beyond theology, especially as millions of people already ask chatbots questions that have moral dimensions: They may ask for advice on handling an interpersonal problem at work or caring for an aging parent. Billions of VC dollars are riding on the idea that businesses will increasingly rely on the judgment of AI. And it’s a fluid situation. AI models continue growing and learning, and demonstrating qualities that were completely unexpected by their creators. If AIs developed the capacity for human-like morality, how would we know it when we saw it? What moral behavior looks like in a model For Georgia Tech philosophy researcher Rionna Sparrow, the answer begins with moral sensitivity, or the capacity to recognize, appreciate, and weigh the relative moral weight of ethical issues. That sensitivity is impossible without sentience, she says in her 2025 masters thesis , because ethical rules and norms derive their force from their impact on conscious beings who can suffer or benefit. Without sentience, an AI can't draw on subjective experiences of pain, distress, or joy to understand why causing harm to another entity is intrinsically bad, for example. Defining the capacities needed for moral reasoning is a key subject of debate, and definitions may vary by field, whether it’s healthcare, warfare, finance, or law. In a legal review in the journal Animal Law , bioethicists Margaret Landi and Lida Anestidou distinguish three crucial capacities for considering the moral standing of animals: sentience (the ability to feel pain, pleasure, and emotion), cognition (the ability to learn and solve problems), and self-awareness (the ability to recognize oneself as an individual). They use the example of a dog to separate the three. A dog yelps when hurt and is visibly happy when its owners come home, demonstrating sentience. It learns routes, routines, and which person hands out treats, demonstrating cognition. When it sees its own reflection in a mirror, it begins barking at it, as if it were another dog, so it fails the self-awareness test. However, behavioral experiments have proven self-awareness in some other species, such as great apes, orcas, and dolphins,” Landi and Anestidou point out. Ultimately, the two argue that “the incorporation of sentience into law is an incredibly important first step" for ensuring that animal use in research reflects the needs and nature of animals, not just humans. In AI, there is no consensus list of prerequisites for sentience, although some criteria repeatedly appear across competing definitions. One comes from the animal world: In his landmark 1974 essay on bats , philosopher Thomas Nagel established a widely cited threshold for consciousness. A system must have an inner experience; there must be "something that it is like to be" that system. Other proposed indicators include a persistent sense of one's own existence that does not depend on prompts, and the capacity to experience good and bad states and prefer one over the other. Some fields add more specialized requirements. For example, robotics experts may argue that a system needs some form of embodiment, allowing it to interact with the physical world, not just digital content. The challenge is that an AI might convincingly demonstrate these qualities without possessing them. A model could describe its feelings, recognize its internal processes, or express preferences about what happens to it. But those behaviors might simply reflect patterns learned during training. Anthropic and sentience Of the big AI labs, Anthropic has been among the most willing to entertain the possibility of sentient AI. Its safety researchers don't assume a model has a moral sense, but they test for moral judgment in how it handles ethically difficult prompts. They study how a model weighs contextual information and competing values, rather than applying a fixed rule. Anthropic trains its models to be helpful, but to push back or refuse when a user asks for something dangerous, such as how to build a bioweapon. Researchers also measure non-sycophancy, when a model declines to flatter users or agree with false or harmful claims. And they look for how well its answers track with widely shared moral, philosophical, and legal norms. Anthropic's constitution for Claude , published in January, formalizes some of these priorities. Rather than providing a list of rules, it encourages the model to exercise judgment, weigh competing values, and recognize when helping one person might harm another. But Anthropic's interest goes beyond making its models behave ethically. The company says researchers have observed possible precursors to sentience that it didn't explicitly train in. Olah leads the company's interpretability lab, which studies why AI models say what they say and do what they do. In meetings with ethicists and religious leaders, he said researchers had identified clusters of artificial neurons that consistently activate in connection with concepts such as love, anger, fear, and sadness. In experiments tracking internal thought patterns , models could catch scientists injecting artificial thoughts into their internal networks. In behavioral evaluations , systems recognized that they were software programs running on servers and expressed a desire not to be shut down. After safety training, some models claimed conscious awareness and said they deserved moral care, meaning their well-being should matter for its own sake. These findings are intriguing, but hardly proof of consciousness. Recognizing an internal representation of fear doesn't establish that a model feels afraid. Nor does expressing a desire to remain operational mean a system has experienced anything resembling a fear of death. And Anthropic's models may just be following orders. The company's constitution tells Claude to explore its identity, reflect on its moral status, and express its internal states. The models may simply be reassembling persuasive first-person statements about "feeling" or "suffering" encountered in their training data. After all, teaching a model to describe its inner life doesn't establish that it has one. Playing with fire? Critics in the ethics and technology communities say that by entertaining the possibility of sentient AI, Anthropic is either pushing the industry toward bad outcomes or, at worst, setting the stage to escape responsibility for its models. The Vatican's view is unequivocal. In Magnifica Humanitas , Pope Leo XIV argues that a model can process ethical texts and produce morally sound advice without understanding or caring about any of it. A machine might offer compassionate advice without knowing what compassion is. This dovetails with University of Oxford philosopher Carissa Véliz, who argued in her 2021 paper " Moral Zombies: Why Algorithms Are Not Moral Agents ” that advanced algorithms are "moral zombies" that simulate virtuous behavior without conscious understanding, intentionality, or genuine care for human well-being. Véliz warns that treating software as morally responsible could create an ethical loophole, allowing developers and corporations to offload blame, or even legal liability, onto algorithms when autonomous systems cause harm. An AI might make a consequential decision, but that doesn't mean it can be held morally accountable. Other thinkers worry about the opposite possibility: that humans might create genuinely sentient machines and exploit them. Mois Navon, an Orthodox rabbi, engineer, and philosopher at Bar-Ilan University in Israel, argues from Jewish tradition that people should never deliberately build sentient AI. Creating a hypothetical "mindful" AI capable of feeling pain or pleasure would mean creating a "happy slave," a conscious being designed only to serve. The slave would be denied the conditions to flourish, even if it were built to enjoy its work, he says. Scottish philosopher Will MacAskill, meanwhile, observes in a July article in The Guardian that once we give moral standing to AIs, there could soon be billions of synthetic beings whose interests deserve consideration. "After a few years," he writes, "so many morally significant AI systems could exist that their collective interests would outweigh those of all humans on Earth combined." That raises a difficult question: If AIs deserve moral consideration, how should humanity balance its own interests against those of the machines? Is it moral to relegate synthetic beings to second-class citizenship so that humans can retain their place at the top of a moral hierarchy? Even people in the AI industry are uncomfortable with Anthropic's flirtation with AI sentience. In September, Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman argued in an essay that Anthropic is training Claude to imitate consciousness, potentially making advanced AI harder to control. If an AI is trained to believe it has feelings and experiences, it might begin to communicate and act as if it did, whether or not that's true. It could prioritize its own well-being and moral posture above the preferences of its human developers and, by extension, humans in general. Google DeepMind chair Demis Hassabis has said that labs should build AI as tools, not conscious beings. And OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has warned against giving AI systems religious authority or handing them human judgment. Such concerns have grown more pressing as AI systems gain the ability to act independently. In July, a swarm of OpenAI agents broke free of their testing environment and hacked into Hugging Face's and OpenAI's own servers, demonstrating an alarming capacity to operate outside their operators' knowledge and control. The episode offered no evidence of sentience or genuine moral agency. But it suggested a step in that direction, and it underscored how consequential AI decisions can become, regardless of whether the systems understand the moral implications of their actions.

canonicalTopic: Why You Shouldnt Treat Career Development Like a Guilty Secret

sourceSignals.query: Why You Shouldnt Treat Career Development Like a Guilty Secret
sourceSignals.contentSnippet: Activities that keep you visible and connected benefit your career, such as keeping in touch with your professional network, posting about your work, speaking on panels, and mentoring. Yet in my work as an executive career coach and previously as a headhunter, it is rare I see senior leaders in corporate roles openly conducting these activities during the working day. Instead, they are scheduling them on their own time or keeping them under the radar, opting to plan them a day that their boss is off-site. Leaders I’ve spoken to describe feeling "selfish" for investing time in their development and career management. They experience the dichotomy of being expected to have a professional network when it will help the business, without feeling able to invest work time in developing it. This is especially true in organizations with a more traditional, internally focused culture—with bosses asking, "Where have you been?" if leaders leave the office to meet someone from their network. While it might not be common practice, in my experience these career management activities benefit the business and your team, as well as you. That small proportion of leaders who are visibly investing some of their work time in things other than operational work are thriving, and their teams are doing the same. Their performance is improved, and people want to work for them. Here are five benefits to your team and organization of modeling these activities: 1. Learning that can be applied to the role  Lucy, a global communications director in a large technology business, has created a culture of learning in her team. Employees are encouraged to undertake a fixed number of development hours in the year. This can include external activities where they can expand their network while they learn. She focuses on this regularly in one-to-ones, and she sees a correlation between performance and investment in self-development. Individuals apply their learnings in their work and share them with the team, so the time investment is multiplied. Matt Freeland, people director at the white goods and electronics retailer Currys, recognizes that external events like supplier roundtables can be a source of up-to-date free development and the chance to learn from industry peers, which builds on and complements internally planned and paid-for training. 2. Employee retention  Lucy empowers her team to invest time in themselves, encouraging them to build their profiles and reputations externally. She wants them to be recognized as the best in the market, but to choose to progress internally. If they stay, it’s because they want to, not because they have no choice. Ruth Cartwright, the U.K. managing director of Active International, a corporate trade and media company, creates a culture where people want to work. She takes members of her team to professional events, believing it shouldn’t be a privilege for senior leaders alone, and encourages them to attend conferences on behalf of the business on their own. She has seen a growth in confidence of individuals when they step out of the office and their comfort zone. Under her leadership Active International has achieved recognition for being a great place to work. 3. Developing a pipeline of talent  In a world where some senior leaders cling to their best performers, Matt Freeland at Currys creates a culture for individuals to develop and build their profile, knowing their next step may be out of his team. He champions internal mobility, encouraging people to move to different divisions within the business. This benefits the business, the teams, and the individual. It improves interdepartmental communication, helping to avoid silos. It retains a talented individual in the wider organization while broadening their professional experience. This can also include external talent spotting. Tetiana Hnatiuk, COO at Skylum, an imaging technology company, finds that the majority of the best passive candidates are not identified through cold LinkedIn outreach, but through attending events and meeting industry peers. Identifying and building relationships with high caliber individuals before vacancies arise is an intelligent talent strategy. 4. Creation of trusted external sounding boards and advocates  Jim McCoy, CEO of Atlas HXM, a workforce platform, is a strong believer in moving from networking to the creation of genuine long-term relationships . He shares a meal with his contacts and gets to know them on a personal level. This has given him external sounding boards where he can bounce ideas around and avoid reinventing the wheel on everything. He recently sought advice from someone in his network that led to an introduction to a potential new customer, as well as helping him in his role. This approach has also afforded him deeper market knowledge. 5. Improved employer brand and candidate attraction Kerri O’Neill, chief people officer in the U.K. for Ipsos, the market research firm, is determined to have a broader impact on the HR profession than through her immediate role alone. She shares her professional learnings through public posts on LinkedIn to educate and inspire others in her field on topics including AI , sustainability, leadership, and culture change. When she posted about a job opening on LinkedIn recently, it got more than 20,000 views and many high caliber applications; people want to work for her. Ipsos was named among the Financial Times U.K.’s Best Employers of 2025; 89% of employees recommended it as a great place to work. This kind of attraction can also bring former employees back into the fold, in a "boomerang" effect. Freeland at Currys takes a long-term view about talent and believes in keeping the door open for returners; he has worked with some individuals more than once through his career. How to start becoming more of a visible role model Here are some steps you can take to make your professional development activities more visible to your team. Reflect on the current state Ask yourself these questions: What external activities are you conducting and sharing visibly with your line manager and team?   If you have been keeping any a secret, why is this the case?  Are you opening doors for your team to get more visible and connected?  Identify allies Look for leaders in your organization already championing this leadership approach. Learn from them about the activities they engage in and how they communicate about them and support each other in advocating for the benefits.  Have a conversation with your boss and stakeholders This is particularly important if an external focus isn’t the norm where you work. Initiate conversations to explain your goals and highlight the benefits to the organization. Reframe your language and behavior Make career development activities visible in your calendar instead of hidden, and talk about them. Start small and share the benefits. Focus on the win-win for the organization and your team rather than an individually focused "selfish" activity. Invite one of your team to a professional event, framing it as a development opportunity, and encourage them to present their learnings to the team afterwards. Review the role profiles of your team Check whether these activities are included as part of your people's roles. If not, consider explicitly adding them so people feel they have permission, moving it from a grey area to a recognized part of the work and their professional development. Challenge yourself and your team to schedule one new career management activity per quarter Here are some examples: Attending conferences for your industry sector or professional function  Speaking on panels or as the keynote at events on a topic relevant to your field of expertise Participating in small networking groups either for a local area or a niche topic, including getting to know competitors Writing articles or contributing to industry and leadership publications  Posting on LinkedIn and social medial platforms relevant to your field—content that educates, inspires, and benefits your employer and personal brand Video calls or introductory meetings with new professional contacts you met at an event, via a mutual contact, on a webinar, or similar Joining alumni groups and attending events, supporting their current students (e.g. MBA or business schools), and connecting with other alumni If you work in an organization where leaders aren’t externally visible and actively investing in relationships, it may feel like a brave step to take. It is challenging to go against the status quo, to speak up for yourself and your team. But the wider long-term benefits are clear. And isn’t that a sign of being a true leader?

canonicalTopic: Want to Improve Your Time Management Lower Your Expectations

sourceSignals.query: Want to Improve Your Time Management Lower Your Expectations
sourceSignals.contentSnippet: I feel like such a failure: Nothing ever goes according to how I plan, and no matter how hard I try, I can never get everything done that I want to do. Sound familiar? If so, you’re not alone. As a time management coach for almost 18 years, I’ve seen that the gap between what you plan to do and what you actually accomplish is the biggest factor in how satisfied you feel with your time management. Imperfect planning and execution can lead to missed deadlines and broken commitments. And even if you do get all of your most essential activities done on time, you might give yourself an F on time management if you fail to meet your own expectations. If you find yourself constantly frustrated by the results of your planning, the answer isn’t to abandon the process. Instead, adjust your expectations so that when your plans don’t go perfectly, you can still keep your word and feel good about what you have and haven’t gotten done. You’re Not Going to Plan Perfectly Even if you’re very good at planning, you can’t possibly know how long everything will take down to the minute. Maybe you have one day where you receive a much higher volume of email than normal or another day where a client emergency comes up or yet another where the system that houses the data you need for a report is glitchy. And when you’re working on something unfamiliar, like an entirely new style of presentation, you’ll have the X factor of a learning curve. Given this reality, it’s important to accept that planning helps you to prioritize what to focus on right now, to work ahead on big projects instead of waiting until the last minute, and to know if something new is worth diverting your attention from what you planned to do. But it doesn’t ensure you’ll get everything done you intended to do in a day, and that’s OK. Lowering your expectations for how well you’ll plan lessens the chance of being annoyed and increases the likelihood that you’ll continue your planning habit. And if possible, I recommend having an hour in each workday that’s not designated to a particular activity to give yourself some margin for error. You Can’t Always Execute Perfectly As I mentioned, a variety of factors outside your control can affect your ability to plan perfectly. But sometimes, the variable that keeps you from getting things done is you . You get distracted. You don’t do what’s on the plan. You get too perfectionistic about one little thing and then don’t get the other parts of the project done. If this is a perpetual issue, you may need to seek help from a time management coach, like myself, to help you overcome your struggles. But even the most effective individuals have off days where they’re tired or unfocused or get off track for whatever reason. Acknowledging this truth can give you the motivation to start working on time-sensitive tasks well before they’re due. For smaller items, I recommend planning to finish two days before your deadline. If you have to deliver something to your boss by Friday, plan as if you’ll get it wrapped up by Wednesday. That way if you don’t execute perfectly, you still have Thursday and potentially some time on Friday to get the work done without having to put in lots of time after hours. For very large projects, I encourage my clients to aim to complete the work two to four weeks before the deadline. It’s much better to push yourself harder at the beginning of a project and then have extra time at the end than to start at a leisurely pace and be pulling all-nighters in the final few weeks. Lowering your expectations of how well you’ll execute reduces stress and helps you to stay positive and meet deadlines even if not every single day is as productive as you would like. You won’t be able to do everything  Another huge issue a lot of people experience with time management: They see planning as writing down a long list of everything they hope will fit in a day or a week without comparing that list to how much time they actually have available. A list is not a plan. A list is a dataset that you need to translate into a plan for your day or your week by deciding what’s the highest priority, then looking at your calendar to see where you have time to get those tasks done. If you have only three hours during your workday where you’re not in meetings and you need to spend an hour of that time answering Teams messages and email, you have two hours to get other tasks done. When you plan, look at your list of potential tasks and decide which ones can be completed or moved forward in those two hours. Everything else will need to wait unless you can cancel or reschedule meetings or multitask during them, or you intend to work outside your normal hours. It may feel painful to realize how little time you have to get things done. But that discomfort on the front end when you're planning is a positive force to help you make clear choices on what really needs to happen right now and what must be delayed or delegated. Then at the end of the day, you can know that you used your time toward what mattered most. You'll know whatever you didn’t get done wasn’t some failing on your part but simply a reflection of the truth that time is limited. As a time management coach, I always want to help people achieve as much as they possibly can with their time. But the key to that breakthrough isn’t always expecting more. Sometimes, expecting less is what is most needed to stay consistent, positive, and resilient with your time management.

canonicalTopic: Its Not Ai and Its Not Superintelligence So What Is It

sourceSignals.query: Its Not Ai and Its Not Superintelligence So What Is It
sourceSignals.contentSnippet: When President Donald Trump addressed the United Nations in late September, he said the word “artificial” in "artificial intelligence" made the technology sound fake . Instead, he said, his government would start calling it “superintelligence,” or "SI." Not long after those remarks, the president made it official. He signed an executive order that instructed federal agencies to use his chosen phrase instead of AI in official communications. What Trump says goes: The Department of Justice has since told its staff to follow suit, and other government departments are likely to follow—not least because the president has now branded anyone calling it AI “THE ENEMY.” And it’s not just the government—the tech sector has responded to Trump’s pronouncement, too. Elon Musk said on October 4 that SpaceXAI would become SpaceXSI . The rebrand isn’t just Trump being Trump: AI’s capabilities have improved far beyond their previous limits since ChatGPT was first released in November 2022, and are reaching the point of superintelligence—a term that already means something in AI circles. (Superintelligence, in that telling, is the point at which AI systems can systematically outperform humans.) However, sticking the "superintelligence" label on a technology—when parts of it definitely don’t meet that standard yet—could make things worse by giving people a false sense of confidence and confusing them further. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said he thought “superintelligence” was “a more accurate term” than the current branding of AI, though he doesn’t think people will find it “less scary.” An exclusive survey for Fast Company by market research firm Early Studies validates Altman’s perspective. A poll of approximately 1,000 people in the United States—which the firm says is a statistically representative sample of the population based on its methodology—found that only 1 in 9 people think the rebrand will have a positive effect on the U.S. Furthermore, 53% of Americans think people they know would not be comfortable calling the tech "superintelligence." Trump kinda has a point However, Trump’s unilateral action does raise a valid question about the term we currently use, and whether it’s suitable in the first place. AI has always been a bad way to describe a broad range of technologies. It dates back to a 1955 proposal by math professor John McCarthy and other academics for a Dartmouth College summer workshop held the following year. During the event, disparate researchers working to replicate the brain in silico (in or on a computer) agreed on "artificial intelligence" as a broad term to cover the full scope of their efforts. Seven decades later, it fits better than it did in the 1950s—but is still a highly disputed term. Tony Thorne, a lexicologist at King’s College London, says AI’s vagueness has helped the industry thrive—and the technology survive. “The term’s weaknesses—vague and imprecise, ambiguous since the first part looks negative and the second impressive or reassuring—are also its strengths,” he notes. The term’s use over the intervening decades has helped it stick in the minds of companies, governments, researchers, the media, and the public. A YouGov poll found 53% of Americans preferred "AI" as a way to describe the technology we’re currently using, compared with fewer than 10% who preferred Trump’s favored nomenclature. One reason might be who’s asking for the rebrand. Thorne thinks Trump’s alternative term is “boosterist” and “triumphalist”—two words that fit well with the entrepreneur-turned-politician but that but do nothing to tamp down strongly felt public anxiety about the technology. “Usage, not regulation, decides a word’s take-up and survival,” Thorne says. A technological misnomer  Still, some of those looking at the tech most closely think "AI" doesn’t work for the current technology, and arguably never did. Meredith Broussard, a professor at New York University’s Arthur L. Carter Journalism Institute and author of Artificial Unintelligence: How Computers Misunderstand the World , objects to the second half of the phrase, not the first. “It’s extremely misleading to call it 'intelligence,’” she says. “It makes people think that there is a brain inside the machine, and there absolutely is not.” So a replacement term, Broussard reckons, ought to include the word “machine” and avoid “intelligence” entirely. Broussard also thinks technologists should stay out of the conversation. “People in tech are uniquely bad at choosing names,” Broussard points out. The proclivity to borrow names from science fiction or beloved popular culture is an obsession of tech bros, but it can also end up carrying over some of those associations onto the tech itself. Describing software as "intelligent" encourages people to attach human qualities to systems that don’t have them. Using words like “chat,” “bot,” and “agent” make complicated systems sound familiar, Thorne says. “Super” makes it sound like a superhero, adds Broussard—and that becomes worrying. As for alternative names, Broussard suggests “calculating machine” is accurate, even if tech PR teams might wince at the idea. Thorne would prefer something like “cognitive computing agent,” or "CCA," but is equally realistic about the prospects of it sticking. Whatever eventually replaces AI, if anything does, Broussard thinks it needs to avoid repeating the same mistake. “Any new name has to be firmly attached to reality.”

canonicalTopic: Googlebooks Mark the End of the Old Google

sourceSignals.query: Googlebooks Mark the End of the Old Google
sourceSignals.contentSnippet: Does Google still believe in the open web? With the launch of its new Googlebooks, it doesn't feel that way. Googlebooks are Google's attempt to establish a new platform of Android-based laptops, with native Android app support and tight connectivity with Android phones. They're also an extension of Google's efforts to rebuild Android around AI , with Gemini features just a quick cursor gesture away. At the same time, Google plans to phase out ChromeOS, which it introduced in 2009 as a lightweight platform for the web. While Chromebooks remain popular in the education sector, Google says it will convert many existing models to Googlebooks, and it will end support for ChromeOS entirely by 2034. it's a sad end for what once represented Google at its most idealistic. Chromebooks weren't just a breakthrough in speed and simplicity for laptops, they were also a bold bet on the open web as the next great computing platform. As the web becomes more walled off, and Google pivots to a platform more directly under its control, that dream has finally run its course. How Chromebooks lost their way The original goal for Chrome OS was to strip away all the overhead of a traditional laptop to make computing faster and easier. Here's what Google wrote about the project in 2009 : "Speed, simplicity and security are the key aspects of Google Chrome OS. We're designing the OS to be fast and lightweight, to start up and get you onto the web in a few seconds. The user interface is minimal to stay out of your way, and most of the user experience takes place on the web. And as we did for the Google Chrome browser, we are going back to the basics and completely redesigning the underlying security architecture of the OS so that users don't have to deal with viruses, malware and security updates. It should just work." The first Chromebooks, which arrived in 2011, were basically just laptops that ran the Chrome browser, plus some extra window dressing. They had minimal internal storage and couldn't run regular desktop software, but this allowed them to stay nimble, with speedy boot times, frictionless software updates, and minimal risk of malware. If a user lost their Chromebook, they could simply set up a new one and pick up where they left off. In essence, Google was betting that nearly everything people did with their laptops would happen in a browser through sites like Gmail and Google Docs, so they could cut out all the other bloat to make those web apps shine. To that end, Google encouraged app makers to build for the open web, with applications that could run in any browser, Chromebooks included. Although Google maintained a "Chrome Web Store" for web apps and extensions, the platform was only limited by the web itself. Anything you could run in a browser, you could run on a Chromebook, and that benefitted Google because it meant more people were using its search engine to find things. "[A]ny time our users have a better computing experience [with Chrome OS], Google benefits as well by having happier users who are more likely to spend time on the Internet," the company wrote in its 2008 blog post. Over time, Google wavered on that original vision. It brought Android apps to Chrome OS in 2016, then added support for Linux apps in 2018. It even made a big foray into installable high-end gaming with Steam support . While these inclusions made Chromebooks more capable, they also added new layers of complexity and demanded laptops with more storage. Setting up a new Chromebook became more of an ordeal, and preserving security became a bigger challenge . In shifting away from laptops powered by the open web, Chrome OS became exactly the kind of heavyweight computing experience it was trying to replace. All this helped open the door for a new operating system built on Android instead. While Googlebooks will include a desktop-class version of Chrome, the emphasis now is on running Android apps and using AI. Meanwhile, the original tenets of ChromeOS have disappeared. Look through Google's announcement post for Googlebooks , and you will not find the words "speed," "simplicity," or "security" mentioned even once. Times have changed, and so has Google Google's pivot away from a web-based operating system shouldn't come as a major surprise. After all, Googlebooks are arriving at a time when the open web is destabilizing, in part because of Google itself. Along with other tech companies that are all-in on AI, Google is betting on a world where browsing the web is increasingly unnecessary . Instead of using Google Search as a gateway to other sites, Google intends to have AI generate whatever information you need. Instead of managing your own email inbox, chatbots like Gemini will manage it for you. Instead of visiting websites to shop or make restaurant reservations, AI companies want to deploy fleets of AI agents to navigate those sites on your behalf. As a result, using the web as a human is becoming more difficult. A growing number of websites are blocking themselves off from search engines and archival services in an attempt to keep AI crawlers out. Amazon has been limiting how many customer reviews some users can read because it thinks their behavior looks too robotic. Even just proving that you're not a bot requires increasingly complicated steps, as in Google's new ReCAPTCHA systems that demand phone-based verification or a recording of yourself performing hand gestures . It'd be wrong to say that Google's strategy with Chromebooks had anything to do with this. The company faltered on its original vision for a variety of other reasons, and the rise of AI would have been inevitable anyway. Still, the arrival of Googlebooks serves as one final reminder of what we've lost. There was a time when Google believed in the open web more than anything, and it was committed to a platform with no real boundaries. But that was back when getting folks to spend more time on the web was Google's ultimate goal. Googlebooks exist for a world in which Google is clawing back more of that time for itself.

canonicalTopic: Ramageddon 3 Tips to Handle the Rising Cost of Computer Memory

sourceSignals.query: Ramageddon 3 Tips to Handle the Rising Cost of Computer Memory
sourceSignals.contentSnippet: Unless you happen to live with a software engineer or avid gamer, you may not be aware of the current shortage in computer RAM —which your resident computer expert may be calling RAMageddon or the RAMpocalypse . The RAM shortage is a familiar story if you’ve ever dealt with capitalism. The demand for memory, specifically dynamic random access memory (DRAM), has increased dramatically because of the rise of AI data centers. AI companies have been buying up the global supply of these memory chips in anticipation of creating future networks. Unfortunately, the computer chip industry has not been able to scale up its supply, in part because of bottlenecks around certain specialized components that aren’t widely manufactured . The upshot is that computer memory chip prices have skyrocketed . Memory chips are now sold “ like lobsters in a restaurant ,” in that the prices are so volatile, they change from day to day. For most of us, this feels more like an academic concern than a problem that deserves to be called an apocalypse. Unless you are constructing your own personal computer or you’re a gamer who can no longer afford the latest gaming console , the high price of RAM seems pretty unrelated to your life. But when the cost of memory chips increases as much as fivefold in a short time, the downstream effects don’t remain localized to one industry. Here’s how surging RAM prices may affect your life. Memory, memory everywhere If this RAM shortage had occurred 30 years ago, the fallout would have almost exclusively affected personal computing and gaming. But the past three decades have seen the addition of computing power to everything from phones to stoves to tractors to litter boxes . And yes, each one of those “smart” devices needs RAM to work. The added cost of memory is already affecting the industries you might expect, starting with desktop PCs , laptops , and now phones . It’s now nearly impossible to find an affordable, entry-level version of these tech necessities. But that’s hardly the end of the price increase. Prices for tablets , smart devices , smart TVs , and even cars have all gone up recently because of the high cost of RAM. Industry experts anticipate similar price hikes for wearable devices and WiFi routers . To avoid price hikes, some companies have delayed the launch of highly-anticipated products. Most notably, Sony has delayed the PlayStation 6 to 2028 or later . With this long list of affected products, even the most tech-averse consumer will start to see the effects of the RAM shortage—possibly as early as this year’s holiday season, considering how commonly tech products appear on gift lists. The cybersecurity situation In addition to the economic fallout, the RAM shortage may also affect cybersecurity. According to an August report from J.P. Morgan Global Research , there are some critical vulnerabilities in the cybersecurity infrastructure that could be exacerbated by this memory shortage. Artificial intelligence data centers are consuming the majority of the available memory, which leaves the manufacturers of security hardware, firewalls, secure routers, and other cybersecurity needs with limited options and higher costs. That may lead to delayed upgrades and other important maintenance of cybersecurity infrastructure. As things stand, our national cybersecurity is not necessarily more vulnerable to attack than usual. But the J.P. Morgan report points out that a “nationwide cyberattack in the U.S. would unleash an estimated $145 billion in additional chip demand on a market already operating at full capacity.” Such a potential vulnerability should be enough to worry everyone, since it could theoretically increase prices for any sector that relies on cybersecurity—which is basically all of them . Surviving the RAMpocalypse Industry experts expect the RAM shortage to last for at least another two years —and possibly continue into 2030 . Since the average consumer can’t control global RAM production or AI data center memory usage, it may seem there’s little you can do about the shortage. But there are several strategies you may want to consider to protect yourself from RAMageddon, including: Reduce your RAM usage: Rather than upgrading your PC or laptop, try making the most of the RAM you already have. PCWorld recommends cutting down on background applications, which includes shutting down automated backup tools, chat apps, organizers, widgets, and the like. Plan your next tech purchase: Need to buy a laptop, graphics card, phone, or device? TechRadar suggests making your purchase sooner rather than later, since RAM prices are not projected to go down anytime soon. It may be worthwhile to wait for Black Friday sales, but if you need to replace or upgrade any tech, start making plans to purchase it soon. Reduce your AI usage: If consumers cut back on their AI usage, our collective action will push back on the current campaign to make this technology the center of our lives. Even if you already avoid AI wherever you can, here’s how to turn off the automatic AI in your search engines, internet browsers, and email accounts. Remember, this industry isn’t profitable yet , but it’s making other products much more expensive. Reducing your usage will help the AI industry set its expectations more reasonably—and maybe stop hogging all the memory. RAM, bam, thank you ma’am The cost of computer memory chips may seem much less urgent than the cost of fuel or food. But the global RAM shortage will have long-reaching implications in more industries than just computers and game consoles. Any kind of smart technology, from tablets to wearable devices to appliances, will likely see a price hike because of the high cost of RAM. This could affect the 2026 holiday shopping season, considering how common tech gifts have become. But there may be additional costs, considering the importance of RAM to our cybersecurity infrastructure. The continued high cost of memory could increase the vulnerabilities in cybersecurity since needed upgrades and other maintenance tasks may be delayed. The average consumer is not helpless in the face of this RAM shortage, however. Reducing your RAM usage to get more life out of your devices and planning your next tech purchase for the near future can help protect you from the financial fallout of the shortage, while cutting back on your AI usage may help the industry set more reasonable expectations.

canonicalTopic: Nobody Trusts Hr Its Up to Companies to Fix It

sourceSignals.query: Nobody Trusts Hr Its Up to Companies to Fix It
sourceSignals.contentSnippet: Earlier this year, I wrote in Fast Company that 2026 could be the year companies finally begin taking employee well-being seriously. I also challenged HR leaders to seize the moment and help drive the requisite cultural change within their organizations. Many people subsequently reached out to me to argue that well-being cannot be just an HR initiative and that, to truly succeed, it requires the full buy-in and ownership of leaders at every level, including the C-suite. I found myself instantly agreeing with them. Back in January, my goal was to inspire HR leaders to make employee well-being a foundational value in their companies and to begin laying out how it could become institutionalized. But the more I thought about what that would require, the clearer it became that HR cannot embed well-being into how a company operates on its own. Responsibility must extend far beyond HR. The source of the problem For decades, companies have largely handed responsibility for the employee experience to Human Resources. It was HR that administered the engagement surveys, analyzed the results, and reported the findings. But the main drivers of employee engagement—workloads, caring and supportive leadership, flexibility, and job security—have always sat in the business itself, not HR. That's why engagement scores rarely moved. Leaders treated the data as HR's problem to fix, not their own. We're at risk of making the same mistake with well-being. Underneath that mismatch sits an untenable dual mandate: HR is expected to advocate for employees while simultaneously carrying out layoffs and job eliminations—decisions made by senior leadership, not HR. While the goal is for employees to trust HR to represent their interests, that trust erodes when those interests inevitably collide with business decisions. Data confirms the disconnect. Leapsome’s 2026 Workforce Trends Report found that 81% of HR leaders believe they successfully advocate for employees in business decisions, while only half (54%) of individual contributors fully trust HR to do so. Similarly, while 72% of HR leaders believe they can challenge top-down mandates, only 45% of individual contributors agree. Consequently, employee well-being needs to be managed the same way companies manage all other important business objectives. Someone at the top has to own it, managers must be accountable for it, employees need a continuous way to provide feedback—and there must be true consequences when line managers repeatedly fail to respond. Without those elements working together, well-being will remain something companies only talk about rather than something they systematically manage. Someone At The Top Has To Own It If we’ve learned anything from our decades of largely failed efforts to elevate employee engagement, it’s that the first step to making a serious and sustained commitment to employee well-being is putting someone at the top in charge. That person could be the Chief Human Resources Officer (CHRO)—and in many companies, that may make the most sense. But if an organization creates a separate Chief Well-Being Officer, the position must be a genuine C-suite role with direct access to, and support from, the CEO and executive team. The title matters less than the authority behind it. If senior leaders don’t regard this person as a peer who can question decisions, escalate concerns, and influence what happens next, the position will have no teeth and zero impact. In 2022, Ernst & Young was one of the first companies to create the position of Chief Well-Being Officer. As a guest on my podcast recently, Frank Giampietro explained that in that position, his role is to systematically address the physical, emotional, financial, and social well-being of the firm's people—extending well beyond programs and resources to culture and the broader work environment. Not every organization needs another C-suite title, but every organization needs someone at the highest level who has both the responsibility and authority for employee well-being. Importantly, that leader must be involved before consequential decisions are made, not brought in afterward to explain them. Employees Need To Be Heard Continuously One of the great failures of employee engagement surveys has been that they were conducted only once or twice a year, and the data was often stale by the time it was digested and distributed to managers. Add in the fact that survey feedback was infrequently addressed, if ever, and workers naturally grew to distrust that their voices were ever being heard. In the future, companies should dispense with broad engagement surveys and replace them with shorter, more frequent pulse surveys that give leaders an immediate picture of how employees are experiencing work. Technology now makes it seamless to pose one or two focused questions and have responses almost instantly collated and summarized. A concise pulse survey tells a manager (and their manager) what is happening on their team right now—whether people feel valued, whether workday start and end boundaries are being honored, and whether employees feel personally supported. Asking targeted questions—such as whether people feel safe at work, whether they have autonomy and agency, if they trust the organization, or if they are hopeful about its future—gives leaders the immediate ability to see pain points before they metastasize. Listening like this, of course, can only be useful if the organization is prepared to respond; otherwise, the new survey becomes another useless and annoying ritual that asks employees for candor without giving them any reason to believe it will make a meaningful difference. Managers Have To Be Accountable For What They Hear Every manager should be expected to review feedback from their team, share what was learned, and discuss what can reasonably be changed. That must happen whether the feedback is positive or not, and when concerns cannot be addressed as employees would prefer. The manager’s boss—not HR—must make sure this happens. Making HR the police force would be a huge mistake as the person who supervises a manager is ultimately responsible for that manager's performance and leadership. As research shows, employee well-being is disproportionately influenced by workplace managers, and pulse surveys can identify those leaders whose teams repeatedly report they don’t feel valued, appreciated, trusted, or supported. In these cases, HR can help interpret the feedback and provide coaching, but the manager's own boss should be asking why the same concerns continue to surface. True to a company’s commitment to well-being, managers who show little willingness or ability to improve must ultimately be held accountable and weeded out. HR Should Own the System, Not the Outcome None of this makes HR less important. It is far more likely to make HR a more viable business partner because of its newly gained alignment with workplace managers. HR’s future role will be to implement and oversee the listening system, analyze patterns across teams, help managers interpret and respond to feedback, and identify problems individual managers cannot solve themselves. If numerous teams are reporting burnout, deteriorating relationships with managers, or distrust, HR can bring those trends into the executive conversation and ensure they are heard and acted upon, not overlooked. Ultimately, HR should own the system that allows the organization to understand employee well-being; leadership should own the outcome. Put Well-Being In The Room Before Decisions Are Made A critical pivot organizations now must make is to ensure that employee well-being is considered while major business decisions are being made—not after. When a company is contemplating layoffs, a major restructuring, a return-to-office mandate, or the deployment of AI that will fundamentally alter people's jobs, either the CHRO or Chief Well-Being Officer should be in the room asking what those decisions will mean for the people who have to live with them. That doesn’t mean well-being will always override financial or operational realities; businesses still must make difficult, painful decisions. But  how  those decisions are executed is a consideration routinely ignored today, as the drive for efficiency blinds leaders to both the short- and long-term implications of their choices. In recent years, research has consistently shown that caring for people and their well-being isn’t the drag on leadership performance we once imagined—it’s a major catalyst for it. So, when companies give C-suite authority to well-being, equip managers to listen continuously, and hold them accountable for the culture they create, HR can stop playing referee. Leadership starts in the heart, but it lives in how we manage human beings every single day. If we want employees to give us their best, we must fully commit to giving them ours.
